correctness.rationale: The greedy-arch lemma is proved by explicit matching and an absent subsequence. The exact unambiguous first-return Dyck grammar induces a three-state rational matrix recurrence; symbolic reduction proves all three exact formulas. Height-two coefficients directly yield an exact Bernoulli perturbation. At height three the unique dominant simple root, separated remaining poles and nonzero amplitude give locally uniform quasi-powers; direct implicit differentiation yields nonzero positive variance and the Gaussian limit by characteristic functions. Actual packaged verifier reproduces three symbolic equalities, independent enumeration through semilength 10, direct subsequence coverage through 6, and exact derivative constants. No inference from finite tests to the infinite statement is made.

originality.rationale: Three materially inspected primary works address bounded Dyck nesting, individual-word arch universality, and general regular-language counting. The algorithmic paper could compute indexed counts, but does not assert the closed height-three rational distribution or the precise transition from exponentially small variance at height two to Gaussian linear variance at height three. The prior all-height Dyck index series sums over nesting heights and cannot infer the conditional height-three series. Targeted semantic searches did not find an equivalent formula. Risk of unindexed equivalent research is recorded.
residual_risks: An unindexed, differently named or unpublished height-three Dyck universal-subsequence distribution may be equivalent.

value.rationale: The nesting-three boundary is naturally singled out in Dyck repetition-avoidance research; the subsequence-universality index is a standard statistic of words. An exact bivariate distribution at the first nontrivial height, coupled with an explicit Gaussian fluctuation coefficient and sharp comparison to vanishing variance at height two, describes a genuine phase boundary in a natural constrained language. The new content is more than applying an off-the-shelf counting routine to obtain a few coefficients.
